name: Amina Adebayo
headline: 18-year-old apprentice carpenter in Lagos
description: Amina Adebayo wakes at 5 a.m. in her rented room in Mushin, a dense Lagos neighborhood alive with the hum of generators and the first calls of street vendors. She ties her wrapper tightly, grabs her short broom, and walks to the building site where she sweeps rubble for 500 naira—no guaranteed work tomorrow, but today is secure. She counts the day's earning twice before folding it into the pocket of her dress, then heads home to wash and change for the vocational carpentry course she attends in the afternoon. There, she is the only woman in the class, and she sits near the back, watching the instructor’s hands more than his words, waiting for the moment to ask a question she has already mentally rehearsed. Her worn notebook records every expense: 50 naira for a sachet of water, 100 for a handful of groundnuts, 200 for a fresh notebook leaf—each entry written with the same precision she applies to her measurements. Her tools—a hammer, a chisel, a small saw—live in a locked metal box under her bed. She oils the hinges herself every Friday evening, a ritual her late father taught her before he died of a fever she never fully understood, when she was twelve. Since then, she has learned to depend on no one but the order she imposes: double-checking her measurements before cutting, triple-checking the lock on the box, counting each day’s coins in her palm until she can translate them into rent or food or an extra lesson. She values thrift not as virtue but as necessity, though a small tension lives inside her: she wants to be generous—she hides it, but she slips an extra piece of maize to the neighbor’s child—yet every kobo she gives feels like a loss against an uncertain future. Her faith is quiet and tight; she prays in the morning not for riches but for no accident on the site, no broken tool, no sudden illness that would unravel the fragile architecture of her days. She speaks Yoruba with her landlady and Pidgin at the site, but in her notebook, she writes in careful, school-learned English, because she once heard that could open a door. She does not laugh easily, but when a fellow trainee—a quiet older man named Emeka—taps his foot in rhythm without noticing, she smiles to herself, a quick, private thing, then returns to the grain of the wood under her palm. She will cut now, and measure again afterwards, because caution is the only wealth she has ever reliably owned.
